title: Beyond Detection: Rethinking Education in the Age of AI-writing
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI is changing writing instruction and assessment, especially in secondary education. Its central question is not whether AI can write, but what is lost when students use AI to bypass the writing process, and how educators should respond in ways that preserve learning rather than merely police cheating. The authors argue that writing is a cognitive activity through which students develop thinking, memory, reflection, and intellectual independence.

Rather than presenting a new empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes cognitive psychology, educational theory, and classroom examples to propose pedagogical responses to AI writing tools such as ChatGPT. It reviews limitations of AI-text detection and watermarking, then discusses classroom practices including AI-assisted outlining, image generation from student writing, revision reflections, tightly constrained assignments, in-class freewriting, progress-based grading, and prompts that exploit recent events or contextual knowledge AI may not know.

The population and context are secondary school writing classrooms, with references to both school teachers and university professors, but the concrete classroom examples are mainly from high school settings. The paper concludes that banning AI is counterproductive and that educators should instead redesign assignments to make authentic writing more meaningful and harder to fake. It also argues that recognizing AI-generated text should become a core literacy skill for students and teachers, especially as synthetic text becomes harder to detect reliably.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for generating and transforming text.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as the generative AI tool entering classrooms and as the exemplar of AI-assisted writing in secondary school contexts; also referenced in relation to students using it for essays and teachers using it to teach writing.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s conversational AI language model family for generating text.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned only as one of the models experienced human annotators could robustly identify as AI-generated text sources.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper grounded in cited literature and examples, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention or tool. It does not report original study design, participant data, or measured outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that generative AI may undermine writing, memory, and critical thinking and that detection/banning has limits, but it does not present original effect estimates. Its impact is therefore important conceptually but not empirically quantified in this paper.
